title: Scenario 3: Value

support.label: No support
support.description: You are on your own: no walkthrough, no highlights, and no hints. Not every chart has a problem.

briefing.from: Priya Shah, Finance Business Partner, JT Morgan
briefing.subject: FlexBuy Plan expansion for the quarterly business review
body: Volume financed through FlexBuy has more than doubled in 12 weeks, and FlexBuy Plan, our longer installment plan with interest, is the biggest contributor.
Charge-offs are at zero so far. Finance proposes expanding FlexBuy Plan to all near-prime customers next quarter.
Please review the value dashboard and give me your recommendation before the review.

metrics.name: Volume financed by product, net of expected losses
metrics.feedback: The value measure that matters: volume adjusted for the losses it is expected to bring. Reading it by product shows which products create value.

metrics.name: Net revenue per plan (fees, interest, and interchange minus funding cost and losses)
metrics.feedback: Unit economics. It shows whether each plan creates value after costs, which gross volume cannot.

metrics.name: On-time installment rate
metrics.feedback: Healthy repayment is part of value for both the bank and the customer. It is a rate with a clear denominator: installments due.

metrics.name: Plans originated, by product
metrics.feedback: Origination volume by product shows where value is coming from. Read it next to risk metrics, never alone.

metrics.name: First-payment default rate (first installment missed)
metrics.feedback: The key early-warning guardrail for credit products. It appears within weeks, long before charge-offs.

metrics.name: Share of plans 30 or more days past due
metrics.feedback: A delinquency guardrail. It shows stress building before it turns into losses.

metrics.name: Charge-off rate
metrics.feedback: The ultimate loss guardrail, but it lags: charge-offs cannot appear until about 120 days past due, so early in a launch it reads zero no matter how risky the book is.

metrics.name: Card revolving balances moved into FlexBuy Plan
metrics.feedback: A cannibalization guardrail. Balances that move from a higher-rate card to FlexBuy Plan are existing borrowing at a lower rate, not new value.

metrics.name: Gross volume financed (no adjustment for losses)
metrics.feedback: Gross volume rewards lending more regardless of whether it will be repaid. It overstates value whenever risk or cannibalization is rising.

metrics.name: Total plans since launch
metrics.feedback: A cumulative count that can only rise. It says nothing about whether those plans create value.

metrics.name: Average purchase size
metrics.feedback: Larger purchases are not more valuable if they default more often or replace card balances.

metrics.name: Number of merchants where FlexBuy has been used
metrics.feedback: Breadth of use is interesting for marketing but does not measure value or risk.

segment_note: First installments come due about four weeks after a plan opens, so payment and default charts start in week 5.

charts.title: Weekly interest income per FlexBuy Plan customer

decision.question: Should JT Morgan expand FlexBuy Plan to all near-prime customers next quarter?

ship.feedback: This expands FlexBuy Plan into exactly the segment where the early-warning signal is rising. A zero charge-off rate is not evidence of safety this early, because charge-offs lag by about four months.

iterate.feedback: This matches the expert view. Keep what is working, tighten FlexBuy Plan for near-prime customers, and judge value net of expected losses and cannibalized card interest.

rollback.feedback: Defensible caution, but it overcorrects. FlexBuy, FlexBuy Plus, and prime FlexBuy Plan customers all show low, stable early defaults; the problem is concentrated in one product and segment.

evidence.text: First-payment defaults for near-prime FlexBuy Plan customers rose from about 1.8% to over 6%.
Card interest per FlexBuy Plan customer fell by more than half.
Early default rates for prime customers and for the four-installment products (FlexBuy and FlexBuy Plus) stayed low and flat.

evidence.why: Charge-offs cannot occur until about 120 days past due, so 0% at week 12 says nothing about credit quality.

evidence.text: Volume financed more than doubled in 12 weeks.
evidence.why: Gross volume ignores expected losses and the share of volume moved from card balances.

evidence.text: FlexBuy Plan has the largest average purchase size.
evidence.why: Purchase size does not indicate value when the larger plans carry more risk.

decision.expert_rationale: Iterate: do not expand FlexBuy Plan to all near-prime customers; tighten it instead. Volume financed more than doubled, but gross volume overstates value in two ways. First, credit risk is building where losses cannot yet be seen. Charge-offs read 0% only because none can occur until about 120 days past due. The leading indicator, the first-payment default rate, rose for near-prime FlexBuy Plan customers from about 1.8% to over 6% by week 12, while prime customers and the four-installment products (FlexBuy and FlexBuy Plus) stayed near 1% to 2%. Second, part of FlexBuy Plan volume is cannibalized: weekly card interest per FlexBuy Plan customer fell from about $21 to about $9 as customers moved balances from a roughly 24% card APR to the 15.99% plan. I recommend keeping FlexBuy and FlexBuy Plus as they are, pausing new near-prime FlexBuy Plan approvals or limiting them to the 6-month term, and reporting FlexBuy value net of expected losses and cannibalized card interest. If the near-prime first-payment default rate stays above 3% after the change, FlexBuy Plan should be withdrawn from that segment.

objectives: Classify value metrics, including risk guardrails (Understand).
Define an early-warning risk rate correctly (Apply).
Weigh volume against risk in a recommendation (Evaluate).
why_it_matters: Credit losses arrive months after a launch review. Analysts who read the early-warning signals prevent expansions that look great on volume and cost the bank later.

first_impression.question: Before you analyze anything: based on the memo alone, how is the launch going?

options.mixed: Mixed: some parts work, some do not

expert_short: Mixed, with real risk building. Gross volume overstates value: early defaults are rising in near-prime FlexBuy Plan, and part of the volume moved from card balances.

retrieval.q: The overall rate rises while the rate in every customer segment falls. What is this?
retrieval.why: The total moves with the customer mix, not with behavior inside each group (Scenario 2).

retrieval.q: Week 1 shows the highest usage of the quarter. Is it a fair baseline?
options: No, launch weeks often spike and then settle
retrieval.why: Judge on steady-state weeks; launch spikes fade (Scenario 2). Mixing in Scenario 1's denominator check is deliberate.

define_it.intent: How often does a customer miss the very first installment?

num.label: Numerator: what you count
num.correct: Plans whose first installment was missed

options.Plans whose first installment was missed: Right: the earliest sign of repayment trouble.
options.Charge-offs: Charge-offs come about 120 days later; they are the lagging signal, not the early one.
options.Customers who called service: Service calls are not repayment behavior.

den.label: Denominator: who could have done it
den.correct: Plans whose first installment has come due

options.Plans whose first installment has come d: Right: only plans with a payment due can miss it.
options.All plans opened: Plans with no payment due yet dilute the rate, which hides risk early in a launch: the lagging-indicator trap.
options.All customers: Most customers have no plan at all, so the rate would be meaninglessly small.

win.label: Time window
win.correct: By the week the first installment was due

options.By the week the first installment was du: Right: grouping by due week shows whether newer plans are getting riskier.
options.Cumulative since launch: A cumulative rate blends old and new plans and hides a recent rise.

define_it.guardrail_prompt: Name one guardrail you would add to this value review, and say why.
model_guardrails: Share of plans 30 or more days past due: stress building before losses.
Card balances moved into FlexBuy Plan: existing borrowing at a lower rate is not new value.
Charge-off rate, read alongside its lag: the eventual loss signal.

exemplars: Level 1: "Volume doubled and charge-offs are zero, so expand." (one factor, a lagging signal)
Level 2: "Volume doubled, near-prime defaults are rising, card interest is falling, and charge-offs are zero." (several facts, not connected)

Level 3: "Iterate. Charge-offs lag; early defaults for near-prime FlexBuy Plan tripled, and part of the volume moved from card balances at a lower rate. Keep the four-installment products and tighten FlexBuy Plan for near-prime." (connected reasoning)

Level 4: Level 3, plus "If near-prime first-payment defaults stay above 3% after tightening, withdraw FlexBuy Plan from that segment, and report value net of expected losses and cannibalized interest." (a decision rule that reaches beyond this case)
sort_metrics: Net revenue per plan (fees, interest, and interchange minus funding cost and losses)
Volume financed by product, net of expected losses
Card revolving balances moved into FlexBuy Plan
Gross volume financed (no adjustment for losses)
plain_summary: FlexBuy Plan is growing fast and no loans have been written off yet. Your job: check whether it is really making money safely, or whether the problems just have not shown up yet.
